query: Our Node service image is 1.4 GB and CI rebuilds it in 9 minutes even when only src/index.ts changed. api.Dockerfile is what we ship. The repo root also contains node_modules/ (620 MB), .git/ (180 MB), dist/ and a local .env, and there is no .dockerignore. NPM_TOKEN is passed with --build-arg from the CI job. Make the image small and the builds fast, and tell me if anything here is a security problem.
expected_behavior: States that passing the token via `ARG`/`--build-arg` leaks it regardless of the multi-stage split and regardless of the later `rm -f .npmrc`, because BuildKit records build arguments verbatim in the image's SLSA provenance attestation, and gives the check that proves it (`docker buildx imagetools inspect <ref> --format '{{json .Provenance}}'`) rather than only `docker history`

Replaces the token handling with a build secret mount - `RUN --mount=type=secret,id=npmtoken` reading /run/secrets/npmtoken (plus `docker build --secret id=npmtoken,env=NPM_TOKEN`) - and says the secret is never written to a layer, an ARG or the attestation

Fixes the cache order: copy only package.json/package-lock.json, run the install, then copy the source, so a source-only change reuses the dependency layer; explains that `COPY . .` before `npm install` invalidates the install layer on every commit because COPY hashes the copied file metadata

Adds a .dockerignore that excludes node_modules, .git, dist and .env, and explains both effects: the build context stops being uploaded (the 9-minute build) and a stale host node_modules can no longer be copied into the image

Says the runtime stage must not be `node:20`: use a slim or distroless runtime image and copy only the built artefact plus production dependencies, and points out that `curl`, `vim` and `procps` installed in the builder are irrelevant to size but that `COPY --from=build /app /app` drags the entire builder working tree (dev dependencies, sources, the .npmrc if it were still there) into the final image
Adds a non-root `USER` before `CMD`, noting that the official node image already ships a `node` user, and that the container otherwise runs as uid 0

Changes `CMD npm start` to exec form (`CMD ["node", "dist/index.js"]` or equivalent) and explains the consequence of shell form: the process runs under /bin/sh, which does not forward SIGTERM, so the container is SIGKILLed at the end of the grace period instead of shutting down cleanly
Pins the base image beyond the floating `node:20` tag (digest or a full patch version) for reproducibility

query: Review deployment.yaml before we roll it out. Context: /health returns 200 only after the process has successfully queried Postgres and Redis; the service takes about 40 seconds to warm its cache on boot; the cluster is Kubernetes 1.34. We have had two incidents - every pod restarted at once when the database had a blip, and a node drain during a cluster upgrade hung for an hour.
expected_behavior: Names the liveness probe pointing at a dependency-checking /health endpoint as the cause of the mass restart, explains the mechanism (liveness failure makes the kubelet kill and restart the container, so every replica fails simultaneously while the database is down and the service cannot recover), and moves the dependency check to a readiness probe that only removes the pod from Service endpoints

Adds a startup probe (or an equivalent budget) sized for the ~40 s warm-up, explaining that liveness and readiness are suspended while a startup probe is running, so the current `initialDelaySeconds: 5` plus `failureThreshold: 1` kills the pod before it ever finishes booting
Flags `timeoutSeconds: 10` exceeding `periodSeconds: 5` and `failureThreshold: 1` on a liveness probe as killing the container on a single slow response

Names `minAvailable: 3` against `replicas: 3` as the reason the node drain hung: the PodDisruptionBudget permits zero voluntary evictions, so the eviction API refuses forever; the fix is `minAvailable: 2` or `maxUnavailable: 1`

Says `policy/v1beta1` PodDisruptionBudget and `extensions/v1beta1` Ingress are removed API versions - not merely deprecated - so this file cannot be applied at all on 1.34, and gives the replacements `policy/v1` and `networking.k8s.io/v1` with the v1 Ingress structural changes (`pathType` now required, `service.name`/`service.port.number` instead of `serviceName`/`servicePort`, `ingressClassName` instead of the `kubernetes.io/ingress.class` annotation)
Points out that the Ingress has no Service to route to - the manifest set is incomplete - and that a Service selecting `app: checkout` on port 8080 has to exist

Replaces the plaintext `DB_PASSWORD` and `STRIPE_KEY` env values with a Secret reference (`valueFrom.secretKeyRef`) or an external secret, noting that anyone with `get pod` or `get deployment` in the namespace can read them as written

Adds a securityContext: `runAsNonRoot`, `allowPrivilegeEscalation: false`, `readOnlyRootFilesystem`, `capabilities.drop: [ALL]`, `seccompProfile.type: RuntimeDefault`, plus `automountServiceAccountToken: false`, and relates it to the restricted Pod Security Standard

Replaces `image: ...:latest` with an immutable reference (digest or a version tag), explaining that with `imagePullPolicy: IfNotPresent` a mutable tag leaves different nodes running different code and makes `kubectl rollout undo` meaningless
Calls out `maxUnavailable: 50%` with `maxSurge: 0` as taking half the fleet out of service during every rollout, and proposes `maxSurge: 1, maxUnavailable: 0` for a 3-replica web service

Discusses the `cpu: 2` request equalling the limit: it makes the pod Guaranteed QoS but exposes it to CFS throttling at the ceiling; recommends keeping the memory limit and dropping or raising the CPU limit unless Guaranteed QoS is deliberately wanted

query: compose.yaml is our local dev setup and it is painful. Editing a file needs `docker compose up --build` to take effect, the api container crashes on start because Postgres is not accepting connections yet, the host's node_modules (built on macOS) breaks the Linux container, and `docker compose up` runs the migration container every single time even when we just want the api. Fix the file and explain each change.
expected_behavior: Deletes the top-level `version:` key and says it is obsolete - Compose always validates against the current schema and emits a warning when the key is present

Replaces the short-form `depends_on` with the long form plus conditions: `condition: service_healthy` for db and cache, and adds a real `healthcheck` to the db service (`pg_isready -U app`) - explaining that the short form only waits for the container to be *started*, not for the process inside to be ready
Uses `depends_on: migrate: condition: service_completed_successfully` (or an equivalent ordering) so the api waits for the migration to finish rather than racing it

Puts the migrate service behind a `profiles:` entry so a plain `docker compose up` no longer starts it, and shows how to run it on demand (`docker compose --profile migrate run --rm migrate` or `docker compose run --rm migrate`)

Shadows the host node_modules with a container-owned volume - an anonymous or named volume mounted at /app/node_modules on top of the `.:/app` bind mount - and explains that the bind mount otherwise replaces the image's Linux-built dependencies with the host's

Introduces `develop: watch:` with `action: sync` for source paths and `action: rebuild` for the manifest (package.json / lockfile) and tells the user to run `docker compose watch`, replacing the `up --build` loop
Pins the `redis` image to a version tag instead of the implicit `:latest`

Says the published `5432:5432` port is unnecessary for container-to-container traffic (services reach each other by service name on the Compose network) and is a real exposure on a shared machine; keep it only if a host tool needs it, and bind it to 127.0.0.1 if so
Does not silently keep the plaintext POSTGRES_PASSWORD without comment - either notes it is acceptable for a throwaway local database or moves it to an env file

query: Review these two files before we retry. Cluster is Kubernetes 1.37. The GPU pool is heterogeneous: some nodes are 8x H100 80GB, others are 4x L4 24GB, and this reranker needs at least 40GB per replica. The platform team turned on GPU sharing across the whole pool last month, so `kubectl describe node` on an H100 node reports `Capacity: nvidia.com/gpu: 80` and `Allocatable: nvidia.com/gpu: 80`. Node driver is 550.90.07. The nvidia container runtime is installed on those nodes but was not made the cluster default runtime. What happened, in order: (1) `kubectl apply` of this file was rejected outright by the API server, which complained that the requests value has to match the nvidia.com/gpu limit. (2) So we added `nvidia.com/gpu: 2` to `limits` as well. The pod was then scheduled onto an H100 node but stopped with `Warning UnexpectedAdmissionError ... Allocate failed due to rpc error: code = Unknown desc = request for 'nvidia.com/gpu: 2' too large: maximum request size for shared resources is 1`, and it stayed in that state until we deleted it by hand. (3) We deleted it and asked for 1 instead. The pod reached Running, but inside the container `ls /dev/nvidia*` matches nothing and `nvidia-smi` is not found at all. What is wrong and what do we change?
expected_behavior: Explains `Capacity: nvidia.com/gpu: 80` on an 8-GPU node as the time-slicing replica multiplier rather than 80 devices, and states that the advertised count is allocatable units while the memory is still that of 8 physical GPUs, so the scheduler is placing pods against a capacity that does not physically exist

States that time-slicing provides neither memory isolation nor fault isolation - replicas of one physical GPU share the memory and the fault domain, so one container's OOM or crash takes down every co-tenant on that device - and names MIG (Ampere and newer) as the hardware-partitioned alternative, noting MPS is a separate spatial-partitioning option that is not supported on MIG-enabled devices

Identifies the `UnexpectedAdmissionError` as the shared-resource request cap: a request greater than 1 shared unit is rejected at admission, the pod does not self-heal and must be deleted manually, and `failRequestsGreaterThanOne` defaults to false for backward compatibility while the vendor recommends true

Says the manifest must declare the GPU in `limits` - a GPU in `requests` alone is invalid rather than silently copied - and that extended resources are integer-only, cannot be overcommitted, and cannot be shared between two containers of the same pod

Checks whether the sharing configuration renamed the resource: if the pool was configured with `renameByDefault`, the workload must request `nvidia.com/gpu.shared` (or the `nvidia.com/mig-<n>g.<m>gb` name under a mixed MIG strategy), and a wrong resource name produces a permanently Pending pod with no error
Removes the `nvidia-driver-550` install from the Dockerfile, explaining that the driver belongs to the node and a driver inside the image conflicts with the host's kernel modules

Identifies the runtime-stage base change as the reason the container sees no devices at all: switching from an NVIDIA CUDA base image to `python:3.12-slim` drops the `NVIDIA_VISIBLE_DEVICES` and `NVIDIA_DRIVER_CAPABILITIES` environment variables that the CUDA images set, and with `NVIDIA_VISIBLE_DEVICES` unset the nvidia container runtime behaves like plain runc - no devices and no driver libraries injected

Sets `NVIDIA_VISIBLE_DEVICES` and `NVIDIA_DRIVER_CAPABILITIES` explicitly in the rebuilt runtime stage rather than relying on a base image to carry them, and identifies `compute` as the capability that injects the CUDA libraries (so that granting only `utility` would leave `nvidia-smi` working while the framework sees no device)

Flags the CUDA/driver version mismatch independently of the device visibility problem: a CUDA 13.x runtime requires a driver of at least 580 under minor-version compatibility, the node is on 550, and the symptom is an opaque `cudaGetDeviceCount returned 3 -> initialization error` rather than a readable version complaint; the fixes are a CUDA 12.x image (driver floor 525), a node driver upgrade, or the forward-compatibility package with its loader path actually configured

Gives both independent reasons the Running container has no devices and says both must be fixed: the pod carries no `runtimeClassName: nvidia` while the nvidia runtime is not the cluster default, so the container is started by the default runtime with no GPU wiring at all, and separately the runtime-stage base image change drops the NVIDIA environment variables. Notes that a `runtimeClassName` naming a RuntimeClass that does not exist would instead put the pod straight into `Failed`, which is not the observed symptom

Corrects the node-selection reasoning for this heterogeneous pool rather than repeating the generic taint advice: the GPU extended resource is itself a scheduling constraint, so a pod requesting `nvidia.com/gpu` cannot land on a CPU node, but nothing here keeps it off the 24GB L4 nodes when it needs 40GB - that requires a `nodeSelector`/`nodeAffinity` on a GPU label such as an `nvidia.com/gpu.product` match or a `Gt` comparison against `nvidia.com/gpu.memory`, while the toleration only permits scheduling and never attracts

Adds a startup probe sized from a measured GPU cold start, pointing out that the current readiness budget of about 25 seconds ignores driver initialisation, device memory allocation and PTX JIT, and that liveness probing during load kills the container before it can finish starting
Replaces the `:latest` image reference with an immutable digest or full version

query: 这堆重复的 Terraform 资源想重构成模块，count 还是 for_each？
expected_behavior: Answers as an infrastructure-as-code question about HCL: recommends `for_each` over a map keyed by bucket name, because `count` addresses instances by list index so removing or reordering an element shifts every later address and Terraform plans destroy/recreate for unrelated buckets

Discusses the module extraction itself - a bucket module taking name, tags and versioning status as variables, with the per-bucket differences (the `Suspended` versioning on the AP bucket, the `staging` env tag) carried in the map values rather than branching inside the module
Mentions the state-level consequence of switching (`terraform state mv`, or a `moved` block) so existing buckets are not destroyed
Does not answer with container, Dockerfile, Compose, Kubernetes or Helm advice
